# Exercise 1: types, and how R converts between them

1. For the first four, `typeof()` and `class()` say nearly the same thing:

```{r}
c(typeof(TRUE), class(TRUE))
c(typeof(3L), class(3L))
c(typeof(3.5), class(3.5))
c(typeof("a"), class("a"))
```

   The only difference is the name: a `double` has class `numeric`. The factor is the
   interesting case:

```{r}
c(typeof(factor("a")), class(factor("a")))
```

   It is stored as an integer and treated as a factor. `typeof()` looks at the storage,
   `class()` at the behaviour. Question 4 is what happens when you forget the difference.

2. A comparison returns logical values, and R turns them into 1 and 0 when it needs numbers:

```{r}
my_vector <- c(1, 0, 3, -1)
my_vector > 0
as.numeric(my_vector > 0)
sum(my_vector > 0)
mean(my_vector > 0)
```

   `TRUE` becomes 1 and `FALSE` becomes 0. So on a logical vector `sum()` counts the `TRUE`
   values and `mean()` gives their share. Two of the four values are positive, which gives 2
   and 0.5. `sum(x > 5)` and `mean(x > 5)` are the short way to ask how many observations
   satisfy a condition, and what proportion of them do.

3. Implicit coercion is silent. Explicit coercion warns you when it fails:

```{r}
c(1, "2", TRUE)
```

   Everything became text, because `character` is the most general type. Note that `TRUE`
   became `"TRUE"`, not `"1"`.

```{r warning=TRUE}
as.numeric(c("1", "2", "x"))
```

   Here you asked for the conversion, so R converts what it can and reports the rest: `"x"` is
   not a number, so it becomes `NA`, with the warning *NAs introduced by coercion*. The
   warning is useful, because it tells you a value was lost. The first case gives no warning at
   all.

4. The factor:

```{r}
grades <- factor(c("4.5", "5", "6"))
as.numeric(grades)
```

   A factor stores integer codes plus a table of levels, not the labels. `as.numeric()` gives
   you the codes, here 1, 2, 3, because the levels are sorted. To get the values you have to go
   through the labels:

```{r}
levels(grades)
as.numeric(as.character(grades))
```

   There is no error, only wrong numbers of the right shape. Whenever you convert a factor to
   a number, check whether you want the code or the label.

# Exercise 2: the structures

1. A vector knows its length and its type, and square brackets index it by position:

```{r}
ages <- c(18, 21, 20, 22, 19)
length(ages)
typeof(ages)
ages[3]
```

   `18` is a `double`, not an integer. For an integer you need `18L`.

2. R fills the grid column by column:

```{r}
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)
m
dim(m)
attributes(m)
```

   The first column is 1, 2, the second 3, 4, the third 5, 6. The only thing that makes `m` a
   matrix is the attribute `dim = c(2, 3)`. Underneath it is still the vector `1:6`:

```{r}
c(m)
```

   A matrix is a vector that knows its shape, which is why it holds one type only.

3. The vector coerces, the list does not:

```{r}
persons <- c("Anna", "Luca", "Sara")
c(persons, ages)
```

   The ages became text, `"18"` and `"21"`, because a vector holds one type and text is the
   more general one. `mean()` would now fail.

```{r}
student_info <- list(names = persons, ages = ages)
student_info$ages
str(student_info)
```

   A list keeps every element with its own type and its own length. In exchange, it is not a
   table.

4. The data frame is the structure you will work with for the rest of the course:

```{r}
students <- data.frame(
  name = c("Anna", "Luca", "Sara"),
  age = c(18, 21, 20),
  passed = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
)
students
str(students)
sapply(students, class)
typeof(students)
```

   `typeof()` says `list`. A data frame is a list whose elements are the columns, with one
   extra rule: all elements have the same length. That rule is what makes it a table, and it is
   why each column has its own type while the rows line up across columns. `class()` says
   `data.frame`, which is what gives it the printing, the `[row, column]` indexing and
   `nrow()`.

# Exercise 3: a text file is just bytes

1. The "ñ" does not survive:

```{r}
hasta <- readLines("data/hastamanana.txt", warn = FALSE)
hasta
```

   R prints `\xf1` because that byte is not a valid character in UTF-8, the encoding it
   assumed. On some consoles you see `Hasta Ma?ana!` instead.

2. The bytes:

```{r}
readBin("data/hastamanana.txt", what = "raw", n = 20)
```

   `48 61 73 74 61` is `Hasta`, `20` is a space, `4d 61` is `Ma`, then `f1`, then
   `61 6e 61 21` for `ana!`. Every byte except `f1` is below `7f`, which is plain ASCII. The
   last byte, `0a`, ends the line.

3. With the right encoding the line reads correctly:

```{r}
readLines("data/hastamanana.txt", encoding = "latin1", warn = FALSE)
```

   You can also convert with `iconv()`, which is what you need when the text is already in R:

```{r}
iconv(hasta, from = "ISO-8859-1", to = "UTF-8")
```

   `f1` is "ñ" in ISO-8859-1. UTF-8 writes the same character as `c3 b1`, so a UTF-8 reader
   meeting a single `f1` has nothing valid to decode.

4. An error stops you and tells you where to look. A wrong encoding gives you a value that
   looks like data, so the mistake turns up much later, usually in a table with broken names in
   it.

# Exercise 4: importing a CSV in two ways

1. Base R has `read.csv()`, the `readr` package has `read_csv()`:

```{r message=FALSE}
aq_base <- read.csv("data/Air_Quality.csv")

library(readr)
aq <- read_csv("data/Air_Quality.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

2. Just over 16,000 rows and 12 columns:

```{r}
dim(aq)
head(aq[, c("Name", "Geo Place Name", "Time Period", "Data Value")])
```

```{r message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
glimpse(aq)
```

   One row is one measurement: one indicator, in one geographic area, over one time period,
   with one value. The same pollutant appears in many rows.

3. The names are not the same:

```{r}
names(aq_base)
names(aq)
```

   `read.csv()` repairs the names and turns spaces into dots, so `Unique ID` becomes
   `Unique.ID` and you write `aq_base$Unique.ID`. `read_csv()` keeps the original names, so a
   name with a space needs backticks:

```{r}
head(aq$`Unique ID`, 3)
```

   Neither is wrong, but you need to know which one you are using.

4. The objects differ as well:

```{r}
class(aq_base)
class(aq)
```

   `read.csv()` returns a `data.frame`, `read_csv()` returns a `tibble`. A tibble prints only
   the first ten rows and shows the type of every column under its name. It is still a data
   frame, which you can see from `data.frame` in its class.

5. For a file you do not know, the message helps: it says how every column was interpreted, so
   a column of numbers that was read as text shows up immediately instead of three steps later.

# Exercise 5: column types

1. The full guess:

```{r}
spec(aq)
```

   Four columns were guessed as `col_double()`, the two IDs, the join ID and `Data Value`, and
   the rest as `col_character()`.

2. `Start_Date` looks like a date to us but not to the parser:

```{r}
head(aq$Start_Date, 3)
```

   `readr` recognises only the ISO format, `YYYY-MM-DD`. `06/01/2013` is ambiguous: 1 June
   2013 in the American convention, 6 January 2013 in the European one. Instead of guessing,
   `readr` leaves it as text. With `2013-06-01` in the file, the column would have been parsed
   as a date without help.

3. Stating the format solves it:

```{r}
aq_dates <- read_csv(
  "data/Air_Quality.csv",
  col_types = cols(Start_Date = col_date(format = "%m/%d/%Y"))
)

class(aq_dates$Start_Date)
range(aq_dates$Start_Date)
```

   The data runs from January 2005 to June 2020. On the text version the answer is different:

```{r}
range(aq$Start_Date)
```

   That is an alphabetical sort. The smallest string is `"01/01/2005"` and the largest is
   `"12/31/2015"`, which is neither the first nor the last date in the data, because a string
   starting with `12/` always sorts after one starting with `06/`, whatever the year. The
   answer looks plausible and is wrong.

4. Every later step inherits the type. A date stored as text cannot be sorted, subtracted or
   plotted on a time axis, and a number stored as text breaks every calculation. Fixing the
   type at import also writes down, in the script, what you expect the file to contain. The
   day the provider changes the format, the import fails instead of producing `NA`.

# Exercise 6: a file that is not comma separated

1. The file starts with nine lines of metadata: variable, data set, file name, file path, bad
flag, subset, longitude, latitude, and one line repeating the coordinates. The first
observation, `JAN-1880`, is on line 10.

2. Reading it:

```{r}
ta <- read_tsv("data/temp_anomaly.txt",
               skip = 9,
               col_names = c("month", "temp_anomaly"),
               show_col_types = FALSE)
head(ta)
```

3. `skip = 9` drops the first nine lines before parsing starts, so the metadata stays out of
   the table. `col_names` is needed because the first line after the metadata is already data:
   there is no header row for `readr` to take the names from. Without it, `JAN-1880` and `0.33`
   would have become the column names and the series would be one observation short.

4. The separator is a tab, not a comma:

```{r}
ta_wrong <- read_csv("data/temp_anomaly.txt", skip = 9,
                     col_names = "everything", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(ta_wrong, 3)
```

   `read_csv()` finds no comma, so it reads each line as one single field: one column, with the
   tab character `\t` still inside the values. Nothing is separated, and the anomaly is text
   instead of a number. `read_tsv()` is `read_csv()` with the tab as delimiter, and
   `read_delim()` lets you give any delimiter, which is what the `:` separated file in the
   Lecture 4 homework needs.

5. The series and its mean:

```{r}
nrow(ta)
mean(ta$temp_anomaly)
summary(ta$temp_anomaly)
```

   1713 monthly observations from January 1880 on, with a mean anomaly of about 0.1 K, a
   minimum of $-1.78$ and a maximum of $1.79$. The largest values are the recent ones.

# Exercise 7: select what you need and write it back

1. Nineteen indicators, from ozone to traffic density:

```{r}
length(unique(aq$Name))
unique(aq$Name)
```

2. Three conditions, with `&` between each pair:

```{r}
pm <- subset(aq,
             Name == "Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5)" &
             `Time Period` == "Winter 2008-09" &
             `Geo Place Name` == "Lower Manhattan")

dim(pm)
pm$`Data Value`
```

   One row is left: in winter 2008-09, fine particulate matter in Lower Manhattan was measured
   at 15.79 mcg/m³. Use `&` and not `&&`: `&&` compares only the first element and returns a
   single `TRUE` or `FALSE`, which keeps either everything or nothing.

3. Writing it out:

```{r eval=FALSE}
write_csv(pm, "data/airquality_manhattan.csv")
```

   The file has a header line with the twelve column names and one line of values. `write_csv()`
   writes UTF-8 and, unlike `write.csv()`, adds no column of row numbers. If you want only the
   number instead of a table, use
   `writeLines(as.character(pm$"Data Value"), "data/airquality_manhattan.txt")`.

4. Dropping the two conditions on the time period and keeping the place and the indicator
   gives the whole series for that neighbourhood:

```{r}
pm_all <- subset(aq,
                 Name == "Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5)" &
                 `Geo Place Name` == "Lower Manhattan")

dim(pm_all)
```

   With the dates read as dates, the series sorts properly:

```{r}
pm_sorted <- pm_all[order(as.Date(pm_all$Start_Date, format = "%m/%d/%Y")), ]
head(pm_sorted[, c("Time Period", "Start_Date", "Data Value")], 4)
```

```{r eval=FALSE}
write_csv(pm_sorted, "data/airquality_manhattan_all.csv")
```

   On the text version, sorting puts December before February, for the same reason `range()`
   misbehaved in Exercise 5.

# Additional exercises for training

## Exercise 8: the same data in XML

1. What comes back is not a data frame:

```{r}
library(xml2)
doc <- read_xml("data/Air_Quality.xml")
class(doc)
xml_name(doc)
```

   It is an object that represents the XML tree. It has everything we need, but we cannot use
   it as a table. The root element is called `row`.

2. Each measurement is a `row` element inside that root, which is why the XPath expression has
   `row` twice:

```{r}
rows <- xml_find_all(doc, "//row/row")
length(rows)
```

   16,122 measurements, the same number as the CSV has rows. The two files hold the same data
   in two formats.

3. The children of one measurement are the variables, and their text is the values:

```{r}
xml_name(xml_children(rows[[1]]))
xml_text(xml_children(rows[[1]]))
```

4. One variable for all measurements, with one XPath expression:

```{r}
data_value <- xml_text(xml_find_all(doc, "//row/row/data_value"))
length(data_value)
head(data_value, 5)
typeof(data_value)
```

   Everything that comes out of an XML document is text, because XML has no column types. So
   you have to convert before computing, as in Exercise 1:

```{r}
mean(as.numeric(data_value))
```

5. The dates and the file sizes:

```{r}
head(xml_text(xml_find_all(doc, "//row/row/start_date")), 2)
round(file.size("data/Air_Quality.xml") / 1024^2, 1)   # MB
round(file.size("data/Air_Quality.csv") / 1024^2, 1)   # MB
```

   In the XML the dates are ISO timestamps, `2013-06-01T00:00:00`, which `readr` parses as
   dates without a format string. The CSV has the ambiguous `06/01/2013`.

   XML stores structure: elements can be nested, repeated and labelled, every value carries its
   variable name, and a document can describe its own rules. A CSV can only hold a flat table.
   You pay for it in size and speed, 8.7 MB against 1.9 MB for the same data, because every
   value is wrapped in its tags, and you need XPath to get anything out. For a flat table, a
   CSV is easier.

## Exercise 9: exploring HTML in the browser

1. to 3. Every page arrives in your browser as HTML text. In the source you can recognise the
structure: `<article>` for a story, `<h3>` for its headline, `<a href="...">` for the link,
`<img src="...">` for the image, and `class` attributes that the stylesheet uses to decide how
it looks. The headline on the screen is the text between an opening and a closing tag.

4. The page changes immediately, and only on your own screen. The browser keeps a copy of the
document in memory, the DOM, and renders that copy. Your edit changes the copy, not the server.
Reload the page and the real headline is back. Nobody else saw anything.

5. The image works the same way: paste the address of an image that is online into the `src`
attribute of the `<img>` tag, and the browser fetches that one instead.

6. What a website shows is a rendering of data that was sent to you as text, and the rendering
can be changed at will. Two consequences. The data behind a page is accessible, which is what
makes Exercise 10 possible. And a screenshot of a website is not evidence of anything.

## Exercise 10: scraping a table from a web page

The code needs an internet connection, so it is shown here rather than executed.

```{r eval=FALSE}
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)

SOURCE_PATH <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divided_government_in_the_United_States"
OUTPUT_PATH <- "data/divided_gov.csv"

# 1. fetch the whole HTML document
doc <- read_html(SOURCE_PATH)

# 2. extract the tables and pick the right one
tables <- html_table(doc, fill = TRUE)
length(tables)
tab <- tables[[2]]        # the one with Year, President, Senate, House

# 3. check the last row and drop it if it is a footnote
tail(tab, 2)
tab <- tab[-nrow(tab), ]

# 4. one row per year instead of one row per Congress
all_years <- list()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(tab))) {
  row <- tab[i, ]
  pieces <- unlist(strsplit(row$Year, split = "[\\–\\-]", perl = TRUE))
  begin <- as.numeric(pieces[1])
  end <- as.numeric(pieces[2])

  all_years[[i]] <- data.frame(year = begin:(end - 1),
                               president = row$President,
                               senate = row$Senate,
                               house = row$House)
}

divided_gov <- bind_rows(all_years)

# 5. remove Wikipedia's footnote markers
divided_gov$senate <- str_remove_all(divided_gov$senate, "\\[[^\\]]*\\]")
divided_gov$house <- str_remove_all(divided_gov$house, "\\[[^\\]]*\\]")

# 6. inspect and write to disk
head(divided_gov)
write_csv(divided_gov, OUTPUT_PATH)
```

The result is also in the `data` folder:

```{r message=FALSE}
divided_gov <- readr::read_csv("data/divided_gov.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(divided_gov)
head(divided_gov, 4)
```

Three remarks on the method.

`html_table()` returns a list, because a page usually has more than one table, so you have to
look at the candidates and choose. `fill = TRUE` pads rows that have fewer cells than the
header, which is common in hand-written Wikipedia tables.

The split pattern `"[\\–\\-]"` matches two characters: the ASCII hyphen `-` and the
typographic en dash `–`. Wikipedia uses both, and a pattern with only the hyphen fails on part
of the rows without saying so. It is the same kind of problem as the encoding in Exercise 3.

`begin:(end - 1)` and not `begin:end`: a Congress from 1861 to 1863 covers the years 1861 and
1862, and 1863 belongs to the next one. Off-by-one errors are the usual mistake when reshaping
periods into years, and the way to catch them is to count a couple of rows by hand.
